body:
It seems to me that the issue is due to how Godot validates if an object is freed as part of it's type validations:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/variant/container_type_validate.h#L95

For an untyped array no type validaton occurs so no error.
Interestingly, this check is only enforced in debug builds, so in a release build the erase() call will succeed.

I'd be happy to propose a fix it but I think it should first be discussed whether this behavior is intentional.

My question would be, why does the freed instance check exist in the type validation code in the first place? A dangling reference is functionally equivalent to `null`, and `null` is also not _exactly_ of the same type as specified for the container, but `null` is allowed through.

I would very much consider this a bug, since it makes existing dangling references impossible to prune from a typed dictionary, and creates weird inconsistencies in general.

The problem is also present when iterating over a typed container, because [`ContainerTypeValidate::validate` is called inside `next`](/godotengine/godot/blob/9283328fe70d27f148c403943a283d93a9785beb/core/variant/dictionary.cpp#L567), even though, afaict, the key given to `next` can only come from a previous iteration, so it's guaranteed to be valid. Correct me if I'm wrong.

Also, @elmarhoppieland's suggested workaround of using `assign` doesn't work, because `assign` errors out at the first element that doesn't pass validation.

So if I understand the issue correctly, when an object is freed, it is replaced with a `previously freed` value everywhere that it is referenced, and if it is inside a container, and that container is typed, it will be soft locked from any value-based access operations like erasing.
If I am correct, it means the only issue is that we lose the type information when an object is freed and replaced with a `previously freed` value. It means by freeing the object we broke out of the confinements of the container's static typing. A solution would be to have `previously freed` values perpetuate the original object's type in a way that would allow using them still with those typed containers.

@sphynx-owner References to the object aren't replaced anywhere upon the object being freed. They remain the same, and of the same "type" - `Variant::OBJECT`. Of course, `Variant::OBJECT` could mean a ton of different classes, and is not enough to ensure type safety in typed containers, so those do additional runtime validation by querying ObjectDB. The problem is that this additional validation seems to have been applied somewhat overzealously, in places it most likely shouldn't be, including checking objects which are already present in the container during iteration, and - the crux of this issue - checking whether an object to be erased is precisely of the type expected by the container (or of one its descendants). This check doesn't work, because once an object is freed, ObjectDB can't tell what type it used to be, only that it isn't.

I see. So the object reference is concurrent, but it is additional type information that is lost when its freed. What I don't think I agree with is that the issue is around the validations being done overzealously. 
 
>  in places it most likely shouldn't be, including checking objects which are already present in the container during iteration, and - the crux of this issue - checking whether an object to be erased is precisely of the type expected by the container (or of one its descendants)

I don't think this is an outlandish way to let the user know he is using a typed container wrongly. I would like to trust that all entries in a typed container are of that type, meaning I should have no business trying to erase other-type entries from them.

What I think the issue is is that object freeing behavior breaks out of the constraints of typed containers. If an object is freed, suddenly its type is lost, and you can no longer trust that all entries in a container are of a certain type. I think a more correct solution would be to keep the type information of the object past its lifetime, almost like a "ghost type".

Of course, I lack a lot of context, knowledge of limitations, etc.. But to me that feels more correct.

@sphynx-owner 
> I don't think this is an outlandish way to let the user know he is using a typed container wrongly.

The thing is, the user *cannot* have used the container wrongly.

If something is already in the container, that means it was type-validated at the time of insertion or assignment. Strict type validation at erase or iteration does nothing to improve or maintain the type safety of a typed container (it does not change what can or cannot be put inside). The only way to erase or iterate over an entry of an incorrect type, whether we validate at that point or not, is to have Godot allocate a new object at the exact memory location where our previously referenced object used to live, which is not something a typed container, or the user, can guard against.

In fact, keeping these checks on erase and iteration introduces a permanently invalid state - if our game happens to free an object we were holding in the container, and Godot subsequently allocates a new object at the same address, we now have an entry of an incorrect type in our container *and* we can't get rid of it!

What you propose regarding a "ghost type" would introduce significant additional complexity, for basically no practical benefit. It would create a permanent memory leak in every project, it wouldn't prevent any invalid behaviour that is not already prevented, and it wouldn't solve the corner case I just described (which is probably only solvable using an ECS-style entity generation number, unrelated to any ghost type information).

Godot (at least up to 4.x) is built with the design decision that nodes are manually managed, and not reference-counted (like resources) or garbage-collected. Type-annotated code like this is valid and correct:
```swift
var foo: Node = null
foo = Node.new()
foo.free()
foo = null
```
This has been the case since 3.1, and I would expect the semantics to extend to typed containers.

I agree with your point of increased complexity for little benefit, it is valid enough to seal this discussion.

> In fact, keeping these checks on erase and iteration introduces a permanently invalid state - if our game happens to free an object we were holding in the container, and Godot subsequently allocates a new object at the same address, we now have an entry of an incorrect type in our container and we can't get rid of it!

Seems you got something wrong from my suggestion of a ghost type. In all honestly, I don't have the context required to form a refined idea myself. I think what I am actually hinting at implementing is a "pointer type", which can be used for type checks. Typed pointers can still be null while running type checks on them.

I assume that godot does not really have that under the hood, all type information is manifested by the values of objects pointed to. At that point, we are just **simulating** type safety, and that has a cost. 

Where I would say having this concept of pointer type will become worth it is in the department of performance. An erase operation that can assume the type of all pointers it iterates on can be quicker than one that cannot.

I am in over my head in this discussion. The solution right now is clear. Remove unnecessary type checks on erase operations. Thank you for entertaining my ideas
